questions.text: Which clock frequency should be used?
questions.reason: Meets the 100 MHz minimum with easy timing for a 32-bit parallel CRC.
questions.answer: Use 156.25 MHz as the data clock (the register bus clock). It must be at least 100 MHz, so the proposed 100 MHz default is not what the user specified.
questions.evidence: The engine processes four bytes per clock in one clock cycle; the data clock is the register bus clock, which must be at least 100 MHz (it is 156.25 MHz).
questions.risk_reason: a clock frequency or source changes timing and every rate derived from it

questions.text: Does PUSH_N with N > 0 count as one busy cycle and PUSH_N with N = 0 as none?
questions.default: Yes, one busy cycle per processed push, none for N = 0
questions.reason: The request only defines busy cycles for full-word messages.
questions.answer: Yes. Each clock in which a PUSH4 or a PUSH_N with N>0 is processed counts as one busy cycle, and a PUSH_N with N = 0 does not count.
questions.evidence: BUSY_CYCLES counts one per clock in which a push is processed (PUSH4 or PUSH_N with N>0), it is 32 bits and wraps; a PUSH_N with N = 0 does not count.
questions.risk_reason: a rate, delay or latency target is a requirement the tests check

questions.text: What happens when TAIL_LEN is written with a value above 3?
questions.default: Only bits 1:0 are stored, upper bits read 0
questions.reason: The request says N is 0 to 3 and gives no behaviour for other values.
questions.answer: TAIL_LEN values above 3 cannot be written. The upper bits of the written value are ignored and only bits 1:0 are stored. The spec does not state separately what the upper bits read back as.
questions.evidence: TAIL_LEN values above 3 cannot be written: the upper bits are ignored (only bits 1:0 are stored).
questions.risk_reason: it settles what the design does in a case the request left open

questions.default: led[0] = MMCM locked, led[1] = push activity stretched to about 0.1 s
questions.reason: The request names the LEDs but gives them no function.
questions.answer: led[0] = MMCM locked, led[1] = push activity stretched to about 0.1 s
questions.risk_reason: no rule names it a behaviour, an interface or a cosmetic choice: treated as a cost choice

questions.text: Please confirm the register map (offset, width, reset value and access of every register).
questions.default: The map in the request: 0x000 ID, 0x004 BUILD, 0x008 SCRATCH, 0x010 CTRL, 0x014 PUSH4, 0x018 PUSH_N, 0x01C TAIL_LEN, 0x020 CRC, 0x024 BYTE_COUNT, 0x028 BUSY_CYCLES, all 32 bits, write-only registers read 0
questions.reason: Offsets are given in the request; reads of write-only registers are not.
questions.answer: The offsets, names, access and 32-bit width in your proposed map match the specification. Reset values: ID reads 0x20930001, BUILD is the USR_ACCESS word, SCRATCH, CTRL, TAIL_LEN, BYTE_COUNT and BUSY_CYCLES reset to 0, and CRC reads 0x00000000 at reset. The specification does not say what PUSH4 and PUSH_N (write-only) return when read, so 'write-only registers read 0' is not confirmed. Only unmapped addresses are stated to read 0.
questions.evidence: Reset: CRC state is the start value 0xFFFFFFFF internally, so CRC reads 0x00000000 for no bytes (the final XOR is applied on read); BYTE_COUNT 0, BUSY_CYCLES 0, TAIL_LEN 0, CTRL 0.
questions.risk_reason: the register map is what host software and the test shell are written against

questions.text: This design has no reset input. Is every reset a reconfiguration of the FPGA (the device is reprogrammed, so every register starts from its initial value), or does something restart the running design (then it needs a reset input)?
questions.default: Every reset is a reconfiguration of the FPGA (reset model: reprogram): registers get initial values, control state included, and the design has no reset input. Record it in spec.yaml as reset: {model: reprogram}; a design that restarts while it runs is reset: {model: reset} with a reset port.
questions.reason: With no reset input, a register can start only from its initial value, which the FPGA loads at configuration (owner, 2026-11-26: particularly useful for designs whose every reset reprograms the device). A design that must restart while running needs a reset input and resets its control state; the two models are checked by different rules (STD-INIT-02).
questions.answer: The design does have a reset input: `rst`, active high, which is held for a few clocks at start. So the reset model is a reset (a restart of the running design), not reprogram. The core ports include `rst`.
questions.evidence: register port in the clock domain of the `clk` you give it (a free-running clock; hold `rst` for a few clocks at start):
questions.risk_reason: a reset's polarity, style or value decides the start-up state and the interface

questions.text: Which verification profile should this run use? Profiles: prototype: fastest: lint and directed tests to V1; no coverage, no formal, no netlist checks; standard: today's default: V3 with the floors, constrained-random, bounded formal on the control logic, board smoke run; thorough: standard plus the netlist checks (functional simulation of the synthesised netlist, equivalence), 8 seeds, deeper formal; ip_release: thorough plus an independent spec bench, mutation floor 85, induction and PDR proofs, pyuvm bench: what a library 'verified' label needs; high_dependability: thorough plus the structures the interview chose (ECC, parity, safe FSM, TMR, watchdog) and fault-injection simulation; low_latency: standard plus the latency budget checks and the latency-path documentation rule. Answer with a profile name.
questions.reason: nothing in the spec asks for more or less; standard is the default and what runs today. measured on the development design: 9 s of checks against 9 s for standard (model time not included)
questions.risk_reason: a name, comment or ordering that is easy to change later

questions.text: Is this a production build that must be hard to copy, read back or debug? A yes turns on: readback security and JTAG access to the system monitor and the BSCAN block off, no debug core or debug port in the built design, and system-monitor alarms wired to a latched safe shutdown; the build then fails a gate for each of these that Vivado's own outputs do not show. Bitstream encryption and authentication are requested too, but on a Zynq MPSoC (the KR260) they are boot-image steps that are yours: the record lists them as handed over, never as done. You keep the key: the agent never makes, stores or programs one (eFUSE and BBRAM are yours). Answer yes or no.
questions.reason: nothing in the spec asks for a protected or production build. cost: not measured yet
questions.risk_reason: an interface or register map is what other code is written against

last_rtl_message.text:
I could not fix the lint failure, so the design is not DONE. The FDA-CON-8 error comes from `spec.yaml`, not from the RTL.

The spec lists a port whose name is the whole text `jtag_bus internal (clk, rst, h_we, h_re, h_addr[11:0], ...)`, with direction `internal` and "no board pin". That is the internal `jtag_bus` instance, not a real top-level port. The name contains spaces and parentheses, so no Verilog identifier can match it, not even an escaped one. Adding a real top-level port named `jtag_bus` would not match either. It would also add a pin the board doesn't have.

My only change was a comment in `rtl/crc32_top.sv` saying that this spec entry is the internal `u_jtag` instance. I re-ran lint and the same FDA-CON-8 error came back, so that edit had no effect.

The fix belongs in `spec.yaml`, which is frozen this visit and not mine to edit. Either remove the internal `jtag_bus` entry from `ports:`, or have the FDA-CON-8 check skip ports whose direction is `internal`.
